look_here_first: Little barley (*Hordeum pusillum*) is an ANNUAL cool-season low tuft. In late winter/spring look for a short straight usually erect BRISTLY SPIKE; local physically archived close-up shows head shape, and Matt Lavin's new licensed group photo shows detached awned units. Now MAGNIFY ONE ATTACHED RACHIS NODE: BARLEYS have 3 associated ONE-flowered spikelets, central usually fertile and two lateral smaller/reduced, unlike paired MULTIFLOWERED Elymus wildryes. Little barley's mature glumes are relatively straight and short (FNA central glumes commonly 8–17 mm including awn). H. jubatum foxtail barley likewise has three per node but very long widely divergent glumes, broad often nodding head, perennial growth. Beware introduced wall barley H. murinum (fanlike groups and often well-developed auricles). Confirm glume margins and a small membranous ligule before species ID; do not use bristly silhouette alone.

best_field_traits: 1 — WHERE: look for a small short-lived native, winter/spring green annual emerging in small disturbed-ground tufts; measure the actual rooted basal plant, not one flowering culm.
2 — SILHOUETTE: terminal unbranched SPIKE, typically short 2–9 cm (FNA) and ~3–7 mm wide BEFORE bristles; usually erect and relatively tight/green-straw.
3 — TRIAD: inspect ONE rachis node with 10–20× lens. Hordeum groups THREE spikelets: the central one usually fertile and more complete, both smaller lateral spikelets mostly sterile.

4 — GLUMES: little-barley glumes usually straight/ascending and ~8–17 mm long including their awnlike length (FNA), with basal flattening on lateral glumes; unlike foxtail's 15–85 mm long, strongly splayed, bent glumes.
5 — AWNS: the FERTILE CENTRAL lemma has relatively short awn (~3.5–9.5 mm FNA; ranges vary), not the enormous silky radiating foxtail-barley glumes.

6 — NO AURICLES: leaf blade/sheath junction normally lacks little clasping ears in H. pusillum; inspect the short membranous ligule and hairy blade surfaces. Erect spike + leaf character alone does not prove species.
7 — FOXTAIL: Hordeum jubatum has usually PERENNIAL basal crown and a broad, sometimes purple-tinted, fluffy frequently nodding mature spike, with LONG outward-bent glumes.
8 — WILDRYE: Elymus canadensis/virginicus commonly have 2 or more MULTI-FLOWERED spikelets per rachis node; one-flowered central + sterile laterals is the Hordeum key.
9 — Avoid mixing terms: long showy bristles around a foxtail head can be GLUME awns, not just lemma awns; record their attachment under magnification.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: One spike rachis node showing 3 spikelets
Awn and glumes plus true ligule macro
crew_field_check: Secale cereale generally has one large two-flowered spikelet at each alternate node, not a barley triad. Introduced wall barley Hordeum murinum makes broader fan-like spikelet groups. Use floret and glume closeup.
morphology_keys.habit: Cool-season annual grass, loosely tufted and usually 10–60 cm tall. Native in Texas at state/ecoregion level; do not presume any fresh county-native certification from this visual enrichment.
morphology_keys.inflorescence: Short usually erect dense terminal spike; at each rachis node a triad of ONE-flowered spikelets, the central fertile and lateral companions commonly sterile. Closely packed bristle-like glumes make the little barley head appear bottlebrush-like.
morphology_keys.spikelets: Central fertile floret with short lemma awn, surrounded at the node by two smaller sterile lateral spikelets. Glumes usually straight/upright ~8–17 mm (broad FNA range); the small fertile lemma ~5–8.5 mm, awn ~3.5–9.5 mm; exact dimensions require 1-mm macro.
morphology_keys.leaf_collar: Small membranous ligule (often ~0.2–0.8 mm), AURICLES absent, and hairiness possible on leaf blades; compare real collar/shoot rather than incorrectly teaching auricles as universal in the barley family.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Hordeum jubatum (foxtail barley; native broadly to much of North America, including Texas in Kew state-scale account; LOCAL Hays status unreviewed) is usually PERENNIAL, with long broadly outward-fanning awnlike glumes (up to 85 mm) and a fluffy/nodding spike. H. pusillum is ANNUAL, with short relatively erect spike, straighter glumes ~8–17 mm and shorter awns. BOTH species have ONE-FLOWERED spikelet TRIADS, central fertile/laterals mainly sterile; this is a GENUS trait. Elymus wildryes have more than one flower per spikelet and generally two/sometimes more spikelets per rachis node. Introduced H. murinum has broad fanlike glume groups and often auricles; planted H. vulgare has robust head/cultivar variability; rye Secale cereale differs in spikelet arrangement. Count a real node and inspect glumes, not merely head fuzz.

field_matrix.where_to_look: Compare one complete fully mature head and an intact rooted basal shoot; magnify outer glumes at one central rachis node.
field_matrix.this_species: LITTLE is annual, short erect tight spike (~2–9 cm), shorter mostly straight/upright outer glumes (~8–17 mm) and a short awned central fertile lemma.
field_matrix.look_alike: FOXTAIL is usually perennial and commonly nodding; long fine awnlike GLUMES diverge widely (often 35–85 mm central spikelet glumes), making a very fluffy brush.
field_matrix.quick_rule: Short erect head with compact relatively straight glumes + annual root = LITTLE candidate. Giant spreading feathery head + established perennial crown = FOXTAIL candidate. Both have THREE spikelets per node.

field_matrix.taxon: Canada / Virginia wildrye — Elymus canadensis / E. virginicus
field_matrix.where_to_look: At ONE central rachis node, count attached SPIKELETS, then examine individual spikelets for FLORET number.
field_matrix.this_species: Hordeum = THREE one-flowered spikelets grouped at each node: middle fertile, laterals often sterile/reduced.
field_matrix.look_alike: Elymus usually TWO multiflowered spikelets at each node (occasionally more), with more than one lemma/floret inside each spikelet.
field_matrix.quick_rule: Count spikelets then florets. Three small one-flowered spikelets at a node favor BARLEY; paired MULTI-flowered spikelets favor WILDRYE.

field_matrix.where_to_look: Check degree of fanlike glume groups, actual glume margins and clasping auricles at leaf collar.
field_matrix.this_species: Little barley glumes relatively narrow, straight, close to the rachis; collar auricles absent.
field_matrix.look_alike: Introduced wall barley commonly makes larger wide-fanning awn and glume groups, with distinct auricles and hairy glume edges in some treatments.
field_matrix.quick_rule: Do not label little barley only from short bottlebrush appearance; magnify triad glumes and true collar.

field_matrix.taxon: Cultivated barley or rye — Hordeum vulgare / Secale cereale
field_matrix.where_to_look: Find full rooted plant, flowering head, a rachis node and mature cereal-size spikelets.
field_matrix.this_species: Small wild annual with dense compact bristly spike and Hordeum triads.
field_matrix.look_alike: Cultivated barley is often taller, stouter and more robust with cereal-grain heads; rye generally has solitary multi-flowered spikelets arranged along the axis rather than Hordeum triads.
field_matrix.quick_rule: Large planted cereal escape or singular multi-flowered rye spikelets warrant checking cultivar/horticultural history and mature flowering anatomy.

not_reliable_alone: Bristly spike or three units per node: BOTH Hordeum species share the triad.
Seasonal green growth: several cool-season native and introduced grasses share it.
Foxtail is native broadly to Texas; do not label it universally exotic simply because it forms weeds elsewhere.
Awn/glume measurements from one distant photograph without ruler.
A single broken terminal seedhead: you lose annual/perennial rooting and floret number.
Simple hairy/auriculate grass collar without actual Hordeum rachis node.

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Little barley — photographed real sheath, real head, and still-missing attached rachis triad
steps: 1. REAL HEAD: gallery panel 0 shows a source-labelled actual short tight green little barley spike. Its two original arrows mark only the real head and visible bristles.

2. REAL LEAF/SHEATH: locally archived panel 5 (Matt Lavin, CC BY-SA 2.0) shows an actual exterior green upper sheath and narrow blade. The true inner 0.2–0.8-mm membranous ligule remains hidden; do not arrow or measure it from this image.
3. REAL DETACHED AWN GROUPS: gallery panel 2 shows actual dried source-identified shed units and overlapping bracts, but does NOT prove a three-spikelet attachment to one rachis node.
4. ROOTED ANNUAL: gallery panel 3 shows short headed stems in a patch, but no one plant's fibrous roots. Collect and photograph one authentic connected rooted plant, if permitted.

5. TRIAD AT NODE: three ONE-flowered spikelets are expected at a barley rachis node, usually fertile central with two lateral reduced companions. Existing loose units don't prove their in-situ positions. Photograph one intact node, scale and later its dissection.

6. LEAF COLLAR: carefully unfold blade/sheath inner junction; membrane ligule should be tiny, ~0.2–0.8 mm (FNA/Williamson County); no current photo certifies it. Show a real 1-mm ruler, don't use finger as millimeter scale.

7. LOOK-ALIKES: panel 4 is H. jubatum (foxtail barley, DIFFERENT species). It still has triads but more divergent awns; compare annual/perennial roots, H. murinum auricle/glume margin, and Elymus multi-flowered spikelets.

8. COPYRIGHT: Do NOT ingest or hotlink Minnesota Wildflowers' microscopic/dissected images or Go Botany's ligule photo; their publisher policies prohibit these uses without additional permission. Link their original articles as study references only.

9. RELEASE: SIX physically archived exact-species JPEGs are recorded, with six exact-species teaching panels (0,1,2,3,5,6) and one separately credited H. jubatum comparison (4). The older panel 1 image has a recorded Git blob but independent detailed pixel inspection is still pending. The two newly archived Matt Lavin sheath/head photographs were source-licensed and decoded by the photo lane. No new ligule, roots, attached triad or measured dissection is established; live Pages/mobile and marker placement still require QA.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST — THREE SPIKELETS PER NODE
field_id_short_tiles.short: On a short erect bristly spike, magnify ONE rachis node: three one-flowered spikelets, not three florets.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Look at the physically archived compact green spike (panel 0) and real detached dry awned groups (panel 2). Actual head rows and long bristles are visible, but no existing image proves ONE intact rachis-node TRIAD: two lateral one-flowered reduced spikelets beside a central fertile one. The detached pictured groups (panels 1/2) lack preserved attachment to an erect rachis node. Photograph a still-attached mature node at 10–20× with a 1-mm ruler and separately trace each glume and lemma awn.
field_id_short_tiles.status: REAL HEAD AND DETACHED AWNED GROUPS PHOTOGRAPHED; ATTACHED THREE-SPIKELET NODE STILL MISSING

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 02 · ROOTED COOL-SEASON ANNUAL AND COLLAR
field_id_short_tiles.short: Now pictured: actual green leaf sheath, but inner ligule and roots remain missing
field_id_short_tiles.details: NEW exact-species source-authenticated Matt Lavin LOCALLY STORED CC BY-SA 2.0 panel 5 shows a green upper leaf sheath and emerging narrow blade on one actual plant. The overlapping sheath and stem can be taught without claiming any visible free ligule. Flora of North America and the Williamson County field treatment both describe an inner transparent membranous ligule only 0.2–0.8 mm long. A meaningful photo must open the INSIDE blade–sheath seam face-on, include a physical 1-mm scale, and separately show auricles absent or minute; outer sheath shoulders are NOT the free ligule. Neither panel 5 nor existing Montana patch (panel 3) shows the real fibrous annual root system. Photograph a legitimate collected live crown linked to the full head.
field_id_short_tiles.status: LOCAL EXACT-SPECIES LEAF/SHEATH PHOTO; FREE LIGULE AND ROOTED CROWN NOT PHOTOGRAPHED

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 03 · MEASURE THE FLOWERING SPIKE
field_id_short_tiles.short: Usually erect spike 2–9 cm long and about 3–7 mm wide before the long bristles.
field_id_short_tiles.details: The existing CC BY Montana head closeup (panel 0), newly archived attached green flowering spike (panel 6), and CC BY-SA 2.0 Montana flowering patch (panel 3) show erect, narrow, densely bristly little-barley spikes. FNA gives spike body around 2–9 cm by 3–7 mm before awns; actual existing images have no physical ruler and do not show a full rooted single plant. The true head is a terminal unbranched rachis bearing TRIADS at nodes, not a branched grass panicle. Record full spike length separately from bristle spread.
field_id_short_tiles.status: PUBLISHED SIZE — FULL SAME-PLANT SCALE NEEDED

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 04 · GLUMES, LEMMAS AND TWO AWN TYPES
field_id_short_tiles.short: Central glumes 8–17 mm; central lemma body 5–8.5 mm; its awn 3.5–9.5 mm.
field_id_short_tiles.details: The real source-labelled detached awned group photo in panel 2 shows long straight bristles, bundled pale glume/lemma-like bracts and pedicel-like stubs; it does NOT prove exactly which visible bract belongs to each original one-node central/lateral spikelet, and has no calibrated 1-mm ruler. The other archived macro panel 1 has a Git blob but its bytes still could not be independently retrieved for precise overlay review. For the crew, photograph a true attached full triad then detach the central and both laterals in order, showing straight glume awns versus the shorter fertile-lemma awn, with physical ruler. Keep existing published size ranges but do not claim them measured from these photos.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 05 · CENTRAL TEXAS LOOK-ALIKES
field_id_short_tiles.short: Foxtail barley has longer splayed glumes; wildryes have multiflowered spikelets; rye has one spikelet per node.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Foxtail barley H. jubatum (panel 4, DIFFERENT species) normally has much wider, more divergent plume-like awn-glumes and commonly a perennial rooted base. Little barley's true head in panel 0 is narrower and commonly erect; leaf sheath in new panel 5 helps establish vegetative context, not definite ligule identity. Introduced wall barley H. murinum often has conspicuous auricles and ciliate central glume margins; these require genuine 1-mm photo evidence. IMPORTANT: even within Hordeum, traits of auricles may vary; never identify by absence alone. Elymus wildryes have commonly paired MULTIFLORED spikelets rather than the barley triad of one-flowered units. Confirm rachis attachments first.
field_id_short_tiles.status: LOOK-ALIKE KEY — MATCHED NODE MACROS MISSING

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 06 · PUBLIC-READY GATE AND PHOTO HANDOFF
field_id_short_tiles.short: FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS — additional licensed sheath photo, critical ligule/triad/root missing
field_id_short_tiles.details: SIX exact-species JPEG files are locally archived: the four earlier photos plus Matt Lavin's true exterior sheath (panel 5) and still-attached green spike closeup (panel 6). Three old photos had prior verified pixel readbacks; an older fourth JPEG is physically stored but its detailed pixel review remains pending. The two new archived photos have source/rights and decoded-image validation. SIX species-matched teaching panels now include credited CC BY-SA 2.0 LOCALLY ARCHIVED upper-sheath photo (panel 5) and intact green head closeup (panel 6); one other-species foxtail comparison is panel 4. NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO: one attached source-vouched Hays rooted annual from fibrous crown to full flowering head; one opened inner 0.2–0.8-mm ligule with physical 1-mm ruler; one mature intact rachis node with central fertile plus two reduced lateral spikelets; separate glume/lemma awn origins and measured size. NEEDS_SITE_QA: source CC BY on iNat photo, existing old panel 1 byte/pixel review, licensed creator notices, arrow alignment and actual rights-filtered Pages mobile display. Minnesota Wildflowers macro photos have special copyrighted reproduction restrictions; Go Botany prohibits direct hotlinking. Both may be linked as research PAGES, NOT copied or hotlinked photographs.
